captions: Part four. Build and run one.
The code is only one component.
Controls make it a trading system.
Now we turn the map into an operating checklist.

The right order is deliberate: test first, limit
risk,
then observe what happens in the real environment.

The real stack starts with market data and
instrument
information.

Validate stale feeds, timestamps, missing values,
and market status.
Calculate the signal.
Convert it into a desired position.

Then risk checks cap cash, margin, exposure, order
size,
and daily loss.
An order-management system creates child orders.
The broker API routes tagged orders.
The exchange sends acknowledgements and fills.
Monitoring compares intent with reality.
A kill switch is part of the design, not
an emergency decoration.
Each hand-off should be observable.
You should be able to answer: what data arrived,

what signal fired, which check approved it, which
order
left, and which fill returned.
If you cannot answer that, you cannot safely debug
it.

A backtest replays historical data under
assumptions.

It should separate train, validation, and test
periods.
It must avoid look-ahead and survivorship bias.

It must model charges, spread, slippage, partial
fills, and
changing liquidity.
An overfit curve can look perfect in sample, then
flatten or fail in walk-forward trading.
The chart is illustrative synthetic data.

Live trading adds current queue position, outages,
rejected orders,

and market regimes that historical tests cannot
fully recreate.
A good backtest is a challenge to the idea,
not a sales brochure.
Change assumptions.
Reserve unseen data.
Stress costs.
If the result survives only one narrow setting, it
is fragile.
